But the promotion could soothe some bad feelings. Live Nation will waive fees on lawn seats for 24 hours, beginning at midnight Tuesday local time and lasting through Wednesday. Lawn seat tickets available this week include concerts by Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith, Brad Paisley and many others, Live Nation said. "They're sacrificing quite a lot of revenue here," Waddell said . He estimated that fees add up to about a third of the average price for lawn seats. The economic recession has not seemed to slow the live concert business, which "considering everything else, is going like gangbusters," he said. "It looks like it could be a really strong year," he said. "People want to go to shows. They want to hear music." Every tour offers some type of promotion, he said, including a lot of $10 lawn seats. "This is a business that's pretty flexible when it needs to be," he said. Live Nation began selling tickets to its own concerts only last year, just months before announcing plans to merge with Ticketmaster, the world's largest ticket-seller. Before that, Live Nation promoted shows but had no infrastructure to sell tickets, and it contracted out to Ticketmaster or others to sell them. The Ticketmaster-Live Nation merger plan has drawn criticism. The Justice Department launched an investigation of the proposed merger in February. Neither Live Nation nor Ticketmaster executives would respond to questions about the merger. However, Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff did talk about it before a U.S. Senate subcommittee earlier this year. The merger "will give us greater flexibility in how we promote, market and sell tickets to events," he said. "It will give us a pathway to alternative pricing and fee structures. And we will be better able to develop new and innovative products and services that enhance the fan experience and make all forms of entertainment more accessible to everyone." CNN's Denise Quan contributed to this report.

Live Nation, currently seeking regulatory approval to merge with the enormous Ticketmaster, is rolling out "No Service Fee Wednesdays" this week. The initiative will strip away extra charges from 5 million lawn seats at amphitheater performances nationwide.

The company maintained that this campaign is designed to boost ticket sales and assist financially strapped music lovers, rather than being a public relations move while its Ticketmaster merger awaits government sign-off. Still, the effort might ease some of the frustration fans have felt.

"People get a little ticked off when they think they're paying $20 for a ticket and as they progress along the various pages of the electronic transaction, they see more fees added along the way," noted Ray Waddell, who covers live music tours for Billboard magazine.

The fee waiver on lawn seats will run for a full day, kicking off at midnight local time Tuesday and continuing throughout Wednesday. According to Live Nation, this week's discounted lawn seats cover performances by Aerosmith, Blink-182, Coldplay, No Doubt, Nickelback, Depeche Mode, Toby Keith, Brad Paisley and numerous other artists.

Additional concerts scheduled for later in the season feature Crosby Stills & Nash, Crue Fest 2, Def Leppard alongside Poison and Cheap Trick, Jason Mraz, Kid Rock & Lynyrd Skynyrd, Incubus, New Kids on the Block, Nine Inch Nails and Jane's Addiction, Phish, the Dead, Rascall Flats with Darius Rucker, the Allman Brothers Band, the Fray and the Killers.

"They're sacrificing quite a lot of revenue here," Waddell said, calculating that service charges typically make up roughly one-third of the standard lawn seat price.

Despite the downturn in the economy, the live concert industry appears unaffected and, according to Waddell, "considering everything else, is going like gangbusters."

"It looks like it could be a really strong year," he remarked. "People want to go to shows. They want to hear music."

He pointed out that each tour comes with its own deals, frequently featuring $10 lawn seats. "This is a business that's pretty flexible when it needs to be," he said.

It was only last year that Live Nation started handling ticket sales for its own events, just a short time before revealing its intention to combine forces with Ticketmaster, the planet's leading ticket vendor. Prior to that point, Live Nation organized concerts but lacked the systems to sell tickets itself, relying instead on Ticketmaster or other companies to handle sales.

The proposed union between Ticketmaster and Live Nation has attracted disapproval. In February, the Justice Department opened an inquiry into the planned merger. Executives from both Live Nation and Ticketmaster declined to answer questions regarding the deal.

Ticketmaster's chief executive Irving Azoff, however, addressed the subject during testimony before a U.S. Senate subcommittee earlier in the year. According to Azoff, the merger "will give us greater flexibility in how we promote, market and sell tickets to events."

"It will give us a pathway to alternative pricing and fee structures," he continued. "And we will be better able to develop new and innovative products and services that enhance the fan experience and make all forms of entertainment more accessible to everyone."

CNN's Denise Quan contributed to this report.

Live Nation Entertainment announced a summer promotion this week that would eliminate service fees on lawn seats at its amphitheater venues nationwide, a move that comes as the concert giant awaits federal approval of its proposed merger with ticketing powerhouse Ticketmaster.

The promotion targets one of the most persistent complaints among concertgoers: the additional charges tacked onto the face value of tickets, which can sometimes add 20% or more to the final price.

## Details of the Promotion

Under the offer, fans purchasing lawn seats—typically the most affordable general admission sections at outdoor amphitheaters—would pay only the listed ticket price without additional service fees. The promotion is set to apply to a range of concerts at Live Nation-operated venues throughout the summer season.

## Timing Raises Questions

The announcement arrives as the Department of Justice continues its review of the controversial merger between Live Nation and Ticketmaster. The proposed combination has drawn scrutiny from lawmakers, consumer advocates, and industry competitors who worry that uniting the nation's largest concert promoter with its dominant ticketing service could reduce competition and drive up costs for consumers.

Critics of the merger have pointed to service fees as a prime example of the kind of consumer costs that could increase if the two companies combine forces without adequate oversight.

## Industry Context

Service fees have long been a source of frustration for music fans, who often find the advertised ticket price bears little resemblance to the total amount charged at checkout. The fees, which cover various processing and convenience costs, have become a symbol of consumer discontent in the live entertainment industry.

Supporters of the merger argue that combining the companies could create efficiencies, while opponents contend it would concentrate too much power in a single entity that controls venues, promotion, and ticketing.

## What's Next

# Live Nation Eliminates Service Fees for Millions of Lawn Seats at Amphitheaters Nationwide

*Move affects popular summer concert series as pressure mounts over ticketing transparency*

---

In a development that could reshape summer concert-going for budget-conscious music fans, service fees are being eliminated for millions of lawn seats at amphitheaters across the country, offering all-in pricing that eliminates the often-frustrating gap between advertised prices and final checkout totals.

## What's Changing

The initiative targets lawn seating—the grassy, general-admission areas at outdoor amphitheaters that have long served as the most affordable entry point for live music. Under the new structure, the price fans see is the price they pay, with no additional service charges tacked on at checkout.

Lawn tickets have historically been among the lowest-priced seats at any venue, but service fees could add significant percentages to those base prices, sometimes representing a substantial portion of the total cost for the most economical seats.

## Concerts and Venues Affected

The changes apply broadly across the amphitheater circuit, which hosts a heavy rotation of touring acts throughout the warm-weather months. These open-air venues serve as marquee stops for artists spanning genres—from rock and pop headliners to country stars, hip-hop tours, and multi-act festival packages.

Fans planning to catch major summer tours at these outdoor venues stand to benefit most, particularly families and groups who traditionally opt for lawn seating to keep costs manageable.

## Expert Commentary: The Economics Behind the Move

Industry analysts view the fee elimination through several lenses.

**Consumer pressure and regulatory scrutiny.** "The live entertainment industry has faced intensifying criticism over so-called 'junk fees' and a lack of pricing transparency," notes the perspective shared by many market observers. Lawmakers and regulators have increasingly targeted hidden fees across industries, making proactive transparency a strategically sound move.

**A loss leader strategy.** Economists point out that eliminating fees on the cheapest seats may function as a customer-acquisition tool. "The real money at amphitheaters often isn't the ticket—it's the concessions, parking, and premium upgrades," one live-music economist explained. "Getting more fans through the gate, especially on the lawn, drives ancillary spending that can more than offset foregone service fees."

**Volume over margin.** Filling lawn sections that might otherwise go empty improves the atmosphere, boosts merchandise and food sales, and enhances the overall value proposition for artists deciding where to route their tours.

## The Bigger Picture

The move reflects a broader industry reckoning with how tickets are priced and sold. As transparency becomes a competitive differentiator, all-in pricing—showing the full cost upfront—has gained traction as both a consumer-friendly practice and a defense against regulatory action.

For concertgoers, the immediate takeaway is simpler: the summer lawn experience just got more affordable, with the sticker price finally matching the checkout total.

# Live Nation Moves to Eliminate Extra Ticket Fees Amid Merger Scrutiny and Federal Investigation

## Concert Giant Announces Fee Changes as Ticketmaster Deal Draws Congressional and Justice Department Attention

Live Nation, the nation's largest concert promoter, announced plans to eliminate certain extra fees on ticket purchases, a move that comes as the company faces intense scrutiny over its proposed merger with Ticketmaster and a broader federal investigation into competitive practices in the live entertainment industry.

The fee reduction announcement arrives at a pivotal moment for the company, which has been defending its business practices before Congress and facing questions from antitrust regulators at the Department of Justice about the potential consequences of consolidating the ticketing and promotion sides of the concert business.

## The Fee Controversy

Concertgoers have long complained about the array of additional charges tacked onto the face value of tickets—service fees, convenience charges, processing costs, and facility fees that can substantially inflate the final price of admission. In many cases, these add-on charges have amounted to a significant percentage of the base ticket price, drawing criticism from fans and consumer advocates who argue the fees lack transparency.

Live Nation's decision to remove some of these extra charges represents an attempt to address one of the most persistent frustrations among live music fans. The company has positioned the move as evidence of its commitment to improving the customer experience, though critics have questioned the timing given the regulatory pressures the company faces.

## The Pending Merger

At the center of the controversy is the proposed merger between Live Nation and Ticketmaster, a combination that would unite the country's dominant concert promoter with its largest ticketing service. Supporters of the deal argue it would create efficiencies and improve services for both artists and fans.

Opponents, however, have raised serious concerns about the concentration of market power that such a merger would create. Critics contend that combining Live Nation's control over venues and concert promotion with Ticketmaster's dominance in ticket sales could reduce competition, potentially leading to higher prices and fewer choices for consumers. The vertical integration of these businesses has been a particular point of concern for antitrust experts who worry about the leverage a combined entity would wield over the entire live entertainment supply chain.

## Justice Department Investigation

The Department of Justice has been examining the proposed merger closely, evaluating whether the combination would violate antitrust laws designed to protect competition. The federal investigation reflects the significance regulators have placed on preserving competitive markets in an industry that touches millions of consumers who attend concerts and live events each year.

The scrutiny from the Justice Department underscores the high stakes involved. Antitrust authorities must weigh whether the efficiencies promised by the merging companies outweigh the potential harms to competition and consumers. The outcome of this review could set important precedents for how regulators approach consolidation in the entertainment sector.

## Azoff's Senate Testimony

Ticketmaster CEO Irving Azoff appeared before a Senate committee to defend the proposed merger and address concerns raised by lawmakers. During his testimony, Azoff sought to reassure legislators that the combination would benefit rather than harm consumers, arguing that the merged company would be better positioned to serve fans and artists alike.

Azoff, a veteran of the music industry with extensive experience managing artists and running entertainment businesses, brought considerable credibility to his defense of the deal. His appearance before the Senate represented an effort to counter the narrative advanced by critics who painted the merger as a threat to competition and consumer interests.

Lawmakers questioned Azoff about the potential for the combined company to abuse its market position, the impact on ticket prices, and the implications for smaller competitors in the ticketing and promotion businesses. The testimony provided a public forum for airing the competing arguments about the merger's merits and risks.

## What Comes Next

The convergence of these developments—the fee reduction, the merger review, the federal investigation, and the Congressional testimony—reflects a period of significant transition and uncertainty for the live entertainment industry. The decisions made by regulators regarding the merger could reshape the competitive landscape for years to come.

For consumers, the immediate benefit of reduced fees offers some relief from the frustrations that have long accompanied ticket purchases. However, the larger questions about market concentration and its long-term effects on prices and choice remain unresolved as the regulatory process continues.

Industry observers will be watching closely to see how the Justice Department ultimately rules on the merger and what conditions, if any, might be imposed to address competitive concerns. The outcome will have lasting implications not only for the companies involved but for the millions of fans who participate in the live entertainment marketplace.

As the debate unfolds, the tension between corporate consolidation and consumer protection remains at the heart of the discussion, with regulators, lawmakers, industry executives, and consumer advocates all weighing in on the future of how Americans buy tickets and experience live music.

*Summer 2009*

Despite an economic downturn that has battered industries from automobiles to retail, the live concert business is proving remarkably resilient this summer, with promoters rolling out aggressive discounts and fee waivers to keep amphitheaters and arenas filled.

## A Bright Spot in a Dim Economy

The concert industry's performance has surprised many analysts who expected discretionary spending on entertainment to plummet. Instead, major tours from established acts have continued to draw crowds, suggesting that consumers are still willing to spend on live experiences even as they cut back elsewhere.

Industry watchers point to several factors behind the strength. Live music offers something that recorded music and streaming cannot replicate, and fans appear to be prioritizing memorable experiences over material goods. For many artists, touring has become the primary source of income as recorded music sales continue their long decline.

Still, the aggressive discounting reflects genuine anxiety in the business. By slashing prices and waiving fees, promoters are betting that filling venues at lower margins is better than playing to half-empty houses.

## The Ticketmaster Merger Question

Looming over the industry is Live Nation's proposed merger with Ticketmaster, the dominant ticketing company. The blockbuster deal, announced earlier this year, would combine the largest concert promoter with the largest ticket seller, creating an entertainment giant with unprecedented reach across the live music value chain.

Supporters argue the merger would create efficiencies and could ultimately benefit consumers by streamlining the ticketing process. The combined company would control everything from artist management and concert promotion to venue operation and ticket distribution.

Critics, however, warn that the merger could reduce competition and give the newly formed entity too much power over ticket pricing and fees—the very fees that Live Nation is now temporarily waiving to court fans. Consumer advocates and some lawmakers have raised concerns that combining these two powerful companies could ultimately lead to higher prices and fewer choices for the public.

The proposed deal is under intense scrutiny from federal antitrust regulators at the Department of Justice, who are weighing whether the combination would harm competition in an industry where both companies already wield enormous influence. Lawmakers have held hearings examining the potential consequences, and the outcome remains uncertain.

## Looking Ahead

As the summer concert season plays out, the industry's dual narrative—resilient demand paired with anxious price-cutting—captures the strange economic moment. Fans are turning out for their favorite acts, but promoters are working harder than ever to seal the deal.

Whether Live Nation's fee-waiving experiment becomes a lasting feature of the concert landscape or merely a recession-era promotion may depend, in part, on the fate of its merger with Ticketmaster. For now, music lovers are enjoying an unexpected upside to the downturn: a summer of shows at prices designed to move.
